executive_summary: This sample is a Latrodectus/IcedId loader DLL that performs extensive system reconnaissance, exfiltrates host intelligence to a C2 server, and injects code into remote processes. It is flagged by 52/75 AV engines and executed via Rundll32.exe. Immediate isolation of affected hosts is required to prevent lateral movement and data loss.
intro_background: The sample is a 60,928-byte 64-bit Windows DLL identified as a member of the Latrodectus/IcedId loader family [ev_0001], [ev_0014], [ev_0018]. It is unsigned [ev_0003] and flagged by 52 of 75 antivirus engines on VirusTotal [ev_0018]. The binary is executed via `rundll32.exe` [ev_0011], [ev_0012], leveraging a legitimate Windows binary to load the payload and evade detection based on process name [ev_0009]. It imports only `KERNEL32.dll` and `USER32.dll` directly [ev_0004], while dynamically resolving over 160 additional Windows API functions (including `WinINet`, `URLMon`, `AdvAPI32`, and `Shell32`) at runtime using CRC32 hashing [ev_0020], [ev_0008]. The sample performs extensive system reconnaissance by spawning `cmd.exe` and `wmic.exe` to gather user, network, domain, and security configuration data [ev_0019], [ev_0021]. It exfiltrates collected system information, process lists, and network configuration to a remote C2 server (`https://host2.example/live/`) using WinINet APIs [ev_0019], [ev_0020], [ev_0017]. The sample also implements persistence by creating shortcuts in the Startup and Desktop directories [ev_0019], [ev_0021], and performs process injection into remote processes using `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, and `CreateRemoteThread` [ev_0020], [ev_0008]. It uses RC4 encryption and XOR obfuscation to hinder static analysis and hide C2 communications [ev_0008], [ev_0021].

key_findings.text: The sample is a 64-bit Windows DLL identified as a Latrodectus/IcedId loader variant, executed via Rundll32.exe to evade detection.
It performs extensive system reconnaissance by spawning cmd.exe and wmic.exe to gather user, network, domain, and security configuration data.
The sample establishes persistence by creating shortcuts in the Startup and Desktop directories and potentially installing an 'Updater' component.
It exfiltrates collected system information, process lists, and network configuration to a remote C2 server at https://host2.example/live/ using WinINet APIs.
The sample uses process injection techniques (VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread) to execute code in other processes.
It uses CRC32 API hashing to dynamically resolve Windows API functions at runtime, evading static signature detection.

command_and_control.body: The sample establishes Command and Control (C2) communication by resolving WinINet and URLMon APIs dynamically via CRC32 hashing (e.g., `InternetOpenW`, `HttpOpenRequestA`, `HttpSendRequestA`, `URLDownloadToFileW`) [ev_0020]. It connects to the C2 server `https://host2.example/live/` [ev_0019] and exfiltrates collected system intelligence, including the computer name (`&computername=%s`) and a list of running processes (`&proclist=[`, `"proc":`), formatted as URL-encoded parameters [ev_0019]. The sample also implements logic to download additional payloads or updates from the C2 server using `URLDownloadToFile` [ev_0020]. During the observed run, the sample initiated network traffic to multiple external IP addresses over HTTPS, with the highest volume of traffic directed to `192.0.2.2:443/tcp` (6,532 packets, 395,374 bytes) [ev_0017].

discovery.body: The sample performs system information discovery (T1012) and process discovery (T1057) to profile the victim environment. It enumerates running processes using the Toolhelp32 API, resolving `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`, `Process32FirstW`, and `Process32NextW` at runtime via CRC32 hashing [ev_0020]. The sample also executes system commands via `cmd.exe` and `wmic.exe` to gather detailed host intelligence. Decoded strings reveal the execution of `ipconfig /all` to capture network configuration [ev_0019], `systeminfo` for OS details [ev_0019], `net group "Domain Admins" /domain` and `whoami /groups` to identify user privileges and domain membership [ev_0019], and `nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts` to map domain trusts [ev_0019]. It further queries the Windows Security Center via WMI (`wmic.exe /node:localhost /namespace:\root\SecurityCenter2 path AntiVirusProduct Get *`) to check for installed antivirus software [ev_0019]. The sample resolves `GetUserNameA` and `SHGetFolderPathW` to identify the current user and retrieve standard folder paths [ev_0020]. These capabilities are associated with ATT&CK techniques T1012 and T1057 [ev_0022].

evasion_antiforensics.body:
The sample implements defense evasion primarily through API hashing and string obfuscation to conceal its capabilities and avoid static analysis. It resolves Windows API calls dynamically at runtime using CRC32 hashing, bypassing the static import table which only lists KERNEL32.dll and USER32.dll [ev_0004, ev_0020]. The sample contains a large table of hashed API names for libraries such as WININET, SHELL32, ADVAPI32, and KERNEL32, resolved via functions at offsets 0x869c and 0x904c [ev_0020, ev_0022].

To further evade detection, the sample obfuscates its configuration and command strings using a custom XOR-based routine at offset 0xae78 [ev_0008, ev_0019]. This routine decrypts strings such as system commands (e.g., 'ipconfig /all', 'net view /all /domain', 'whoami /groups') and network endpoints (e.g., 'https://host2.example/live/') at execution time [ev_0019, ev_0021]. The sample also encrypts data using RC4 PRGA at offset 0xcaac and hashes data using CRC32 and FNV at offsets 0x6aa4 and 0xc99c respectively [ev_0008].

The sample attempts to hide its artifacts by deleting its own file after execution using DeleteFileW, resolved via API hashing [ev_0020, ev_0022]. It also uses VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread to inject code into remote processes, a technique often used to evade detection by hiding malicious code in legitimate process memory [ev_0008, ev_0020, ev_0022]. The sample is unsigned and lacks a valid signature, which may be an attempt to bypass integrity checks or simply a characteristic of the build process [ev_0003, ev_0004].

packing_obfuscation.body: The sample is an unsigned 64-bit Windows DLL (60,928 bytes) with no packer signatures detected in the PE header [ev_0001], [ev_0003], [ev_0004]. Despite the absence of a traditional packer, the binary employs significant code-level obfuscation to hinder static analysis and evade detection. Capa identifies the use of RC4 encryption (PRGA) for data protection and the presence of obfuscated stack strings [ev_0008]. The sample utilizes a custom XOR-based encoding scheme (XOR8 rolling header) to encrypt strings and data blobs within its data sections, which are decoded at runtime by routines such as the one at 0xae78 [ev_0021]. Additionally, the binary implements CRC32 hashing and FNV hashing for data integrity or obfuscation purposes [ev_0008]. The sample also resolves API functions dynamically by parsing PE exports and hashing function names (e.g., using CRC32 on ASCII/UTF-16 strings) rather than relying on standard static imports, further complicating analysis [ev_0008], [ev_0020].

payloads.body: The sample is a Windows PE DLL (60,928 bytes) that does not drop files to disk during the observed execution [ev_0015]. It functions as a loader/stage for the Latrodectus/IcedId family [ev_0014], [ev_0018]. The binary contains strings and capabilities indicating it is designed to download additional payloads or updates from a remote server [ev_0019], [ev_0020]. Specifically, it resolves `URLDownloadToFileW` and `URLDownloadToFileA` from `urlmon.dll` [ev_0020] and contains the URL `https://host2.example/live/` [ev_0019]. The sample also includes strings for file extensions `.dll` and `.exe` (`%s%d.dll`, `%s%d.exe`) and an `Updater` mechanism (`Update_%x`, `Custom_update`) [ev_0019], [ev_0021], which suggests it is prepared to write downloaded payloads to disk, although no files were actually dropped in this run [ev_0015].

string_resolution.body: The sample is a 64-bit Windows DLL that relies on dynamic API resolution to evade static analysis and signature-based detection. It imports only KERNEL32.dll and USER32.dll directly [ev_0004], while resolving over 100 additional functions from libraries such as WinINet, URLMon, AdvAPI32, and Shell32 at runtime [ev_0020]. The resolution mechanism uses CRC32 hashing [ev_0020], a technique identified by Capa as "resolve function by parsing PE exports" [ev_0008]. The resolved hashes include functions from kernel32.dll (e.g., VirtualAllocEx, CreateRemoteThread), wininet.dll (e.g., InternetOpenW, HttpSendRequestA), and urlmon.dll (e.g., URLDownloadToFileW) [ev_0020]. This dynamic resolution allows the sample to hide its full API usage from static import tables [ev_0004, ev_0020].
